one_liner: Go-style M:N process scheduler for C (GCC plugin, x86-64 Linux); about 10x faster than Go 1.14 at spawning short-lived tasks.
what_it_does: libcsp gives C programs Go-like concurrency: `async(f(...))` starts a lightweight process, `sync(f(); g())` starts several and waits for all of them, plus lock-free channels, mutexes, timers and an epoll-based netpoll. Functions run as processes are marked `proc`. It is not a drop-in for anything: code is compiled with a GCC plugin, then `cspcli analyze` generates a config.c with per-process stack sizes that is linked with -lcsp.
how_it_is_fast: Stacks are sized at compile time: the GCC plugin records every function's frame size and the call graph, cspcli computes each process's worst-case stack and rounds it to 4 KiB pages, so spawning is a page-span allocation from a per-core lock-free heap plus a hand-written assembly context switch. New processes are pushed to the front of the core's local run queue and popped from the front (LIFO), so divide-and-conquer work runs depth-first and only about tree-depth processes per core are alive at once; idle cores take half of a busy core's queue.
when_to_use: Linux x86-64 C code built with GCC 8 or later that spawns millions of short-lived tasks, such as recursive divide-and-conquer or fan-out/fan-in pipelines.
Workloads where per-task memory matters: compile-time stack sizing plus depth-first scheduling kept the benchmark at 0.2-2.3% of an 8 GB machine against Go's 28-31%.
C network services that want goroutine-style blocking code over epoll (netpoll) and timers without writing callbacks.
Experiments with compile-time stack analysis as an alternative to growable or fixed-size coroutine stacks.
when_not_to_use: Any compiler other than GCC, any language other than C, or any target other than x86-64 Linux: the install docs list only that combination.

Code with recursion inside a process, VLAs or alloca, function pointers, or heavy calls into external libraries: frames the plugin cannot see (dynamic frames, functions not compiled with it, such as libc) are charged a 2 KB default, and there are no guard pages, so an overflow silently corrupts a neighbouring process.
Programs that need select over several channels: open issue #14 asks for it with no reply; and block() can hang main (open issue #16, Sep 2022).
Production use needing support: single author, last code release 0.0.2 (January 2021), commits since then are docs and typo fixes, last commit 2023-06-30.

Processes that share an address space with other code reserving large fixed regions: the allocator mmaps with MAP_FIXED at hard-coded addresses ((core+1) x 64 GiB), which replaces any existing mapping there (not documented).

integration.form: shared lib (libcsp.so) plus a GCC plugin (libcspplugin.so) and the cspcli build tool; autotools install
integration.dependencies: GCC plugin development headers (gcc-N-plugin-dev or gcc-plugin-devel), pthreads; valgrind optional
integration.thread_safety: Multi-core M:N scheduler with one worker per configured core (set at build time with cspcli --cpu-cores); channels are lock-free and a mutex type is provided; blocking system calls must be wrapped in block() so the core is handed off.

gotchas: Harness flaw (scheduling order, not just spawn cost): Go 1.14's `go` statement puts the new goroutine in runnext and kicks the previous one to the tail of a FIFO run queue (runtime/proc.go runqput), so the benchmark's left children queue up shallowest-first and the tree is expanded broadly; libcsp pushes and pops at the front of its run queue and runs the tree depth-first. Go's 28-31% memory (about 2.3-2.6 GB of 8 GB, consistent with roughly a million live goroutines at the 2 KB minimum stack, derived from page data) and part of its time come from this order, from sync.WaitGroup parking and from closures that escape to the heap and feed the GC; per spawn the run costs about 152 ns for libcsp versus 1.56 us for Go on 1 core (derived from page data), while libdill's own table puts Go goroutine create+terminate near 237 ns on other hardware. Neither side uses a sequential cutoff, and a cutoff version was not measured.

The benchmark is otherwise honest: both programs print the correct sum 50000005000000, so the work is not optimised away, and both scale similarly from 1 to 8 cores (libcsp 4.2x, Go 3.9x, derived from page data).

Stack sizes come from the build: every source file with processes must go through the plugin, cspcli analyze must run before the final link, and the core count is baked into config.c, so a binary built for 4 cores uses at most 4 even on a larger machine.

The allocator calls exit(EXIT_FAILURE) without a message when a core's 64 GiB heap range is exhausted or mmap fails, and csp_proc_new exits the program on allocation failure instead of returning an error.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick libcsp over libdill or libmill when you need the scheduler to use several cores and can live with GCC on x86-64 Linux; libdill and libmill are single-threaded but portable and measured against Go too (libdill create+terminate 44 ns vs Go 237 ns). For plain fork-join parallelism Coros or oneTBB-style work stealing is the more standard choice, and minicoro or libaco fit when you only need fast single-threaded context switches.
verified_claims_summary: The author's docs page times sum(0, 10^7) with two child processes per node (about 2 x 10^7 spawns per round, 10 rounds) on an unnamed 8-core, 8 GB Ubuntu 18.04 machine, GCC 8.3.0 -O3 with the libcsp plugin versus Go 1.14 defaults: 3.05 s versus 31.1 s per round on 1 core and 0.73 s versus 8.03 s on 8 cores, about 10-13x. It measures task create-schedule-destroy cost under each runtime's scheduling order, not application throughput.
status_note: Abandoned (last commit 2023-06-30, last code change January 2021, version 0.0.2; the repository now lives under github.com/yann-shi/libcsp, the shiyanhui URL redirects there) but MIT-licensed and small; usable only where a GCC-plugin build on x86-64 Linux is acceptable.
